intro: A fifth-grade store sells every pencil it has by ten o'clock. A truck of corn leaves a farm near Peoria and ends up on a ship bound for Japan. Both stories are about the same two questions. Why can't everyone have everything they want? And why do people in different places make, grow and buy such different things?

The first chapter is about money and choices. You will meet producers and consumers, learn why a price goes up when something runs out, and see what banks, taxes and budgets are for. You will find out why Illinois grows corn while Florida grows oranges, and why trading makes both places better off.

The second chapter is about the land itself. You will learn to read a map with latitude, longitude and scale. Then you will travel through the five regions of the United States, from the rocky Northeast to the deserts of the Southwest, and look closely at the Midwest and Illinois. By the end, you will be able to explain how the land under a place shapes the jobs, food and dangers of the people who live there.
bigQuestion: How do scarce resources and the shape of the land decide what people make, trade and do where they live?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, explaining how markets and self-interest feed a city
Congress orders the land north of the Ohio River measured into square townships, the grid you see from a plane over Illinois
The Louisiana Purchase makes the whole Mississippi River an American highway to the sea
Illinois becomes a state, with a straight northern border drawn to include the shore of Lake Michigan
The Illinois and Michigan Canal opens, linking Lake Michigan to the Illinois River by water
The first railroad across the whole country is finished, tying the West to the Midwest and East
Katharine Lee Bates publishes America the Beautiful after a train trip across the regions
After thousands of banks close, the government begins insuring savers' bank accounts
Congress funds the Interstate Highway System, the roads that now carry trucks between regions
The Mississippi River floods for months, covering farms and towns along the Illinois shore
The census counts about 12.8 million people in Illinois, most of them in the Chicago area

words.d: a person or business that makes goods or does services that others want
a person who buys or uses goods and services
not having enough of something to do everything people want
the next best thing you give up when you make a choice
how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a price
how much of something people want and are able to buy at a price
something everyone can use and share, like a road or a park, that taxes pay for
focusing on making the thing you can do best
lines that measure how far north or south a place is from the equator
an area where the places share features like land, weather or history
something useful found in nature, like soil, water, trees, fish or oil
a center where many routes come together

test.q: A truck driver carries bread to a store. What is the driver?
test.why: The driver does work others want, so the driver is a producer of a service.

test.q: Which of these is a service?
test.why: A service is work done for someone else. A bus ride is work the driver does for you.

test.q: Jalen picks basketball over piano for his free hour. What is the piano practice?
test.why: The opportunity cost is the next best thing given up when you choose.

test.q: When the price of a good goes down, what usually happens to demand?
test.why: Lower prices lead people to buy more. That is the pattern the lesson calls a law.

test.q: The school store had few pencils and many buyers. What did that cause?
test.why: A shortage happens when buyers want more than sellers have at that price.

test.q: Why does a savings account grow a little each year?
choices: The bank pays interest to savers
test.why: Banks lend savers' money and share some of the interest with the savers.

test.q: Which of these is paid for by taxes and shared by everyone?
test.why: Fire protection is a public good. Taxes pay for it and everyone is protected.

test.q: Why does Florida, not Illinois, grow oranges?
test.why: Orange trees die in a hard freeze, and Florida winters stay warm.

test.q: Sam trades extra grapes for Leo's extra crackers. What is true?
test.why: Trade lets each person give up an extra and get something wanted, so both gain.

test.q: Chicago is at about forty-two degrees north. What kind of line is that?
test.why: Latitude measures degrees north or south of the equator.

test.q: Which map shows mountains and rivers but no state lines?
test.why: A physical map shows what nature made, not the borders people drew.

test.q: Which region is flat, has rich soil and grows corn and soybeans?
test.why: Glaciers left the Midwest flat with dark soil, making it the nation's grain heartland.

test.q: Which region has the Grand Canyon, deserts and the Rio Grande?
test.why: The Southwest is mostly dry, with the Colorado River's Grand Canyon and the Rio Grande border.

test.q: Why does Illinois corn travel by barge instead of truck the whole way?
choices: Barges move heavy loads for the least cost
test.why: One barge carries as much as about sixty trucks, so it is the cheapest way to move grain.

test.q: Why do Illinois schools practice tornado drills?
choices: Drills are required in every country
Tornadoes are the hazard most likely in Illinois
test.why: People prepare for the hazard most likely in their region, and the Midwest gets tornadoes.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Is Illinois a better place for a farm or for a big city? Use evidence from both chapters, such as the soil, the rivers, the climate, Chicago's railroads and what prices and trade do, to support your claim.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that says your claim: farm, city or both.
Use at least two facts from the reading as evidence, like the glacier soil, the Illinois Waterway or the railroads that meet in Chicago.
Explain your reasoning: tell why each fact supports your claim, not just what the fact is.
Give the other side one fair sentence. What would someone who disagrees say?
End by saying what the land and the market together make possible in Illinois.

title: Money, Markets and Regions

chapters.title: Producers, Consumers and Choices
chapters.bigQuestion: Why can't we have everything we want, and how do people decide what to make, buy and share?

story.title: The Day the Pencils Ran Out
story.kicker: A fifth-grade store sells out in one morning, and the class discovers what a price is for.
paragraphs: Room 210 runs a small store. Every Friday morning the fifth graders sell pencils, erasers and notebooks from a table by the door. Maya keeps the money box. Devon counts the stock. A pencil costs ten cents. Most Fridays the store is quiet and the class makes a few dollars for a field trip.

One Friday in October, a big test is coming. Everyone wants a new pencil. By nine-thirty the line runs down the hall. By ten o'clock the tray is empty. Devon holds it up. "We are out," he says. Kids groan. Some walk away with nothing, and a few of them have a test in an hour.

At the class meeting, Ms. Alvarez asks one question. "Why did we run out?" Maya says they only ordered two hundred pencils. Devon says they should have ordered more. Priya says something different. "We sold them too cheap. Everybody bought three. Nobody needs three pencils."

The class argues about it. If a pencil cost twenty-five cents, fewer kids would grab three. The pencils would last all morning. But some kids only have a dime. Is a higher price fair to them? Ms. Alvarez smiles. "You are doing economics right now," she says.

The next Friday the class tries something new. They order four hundred pencils and set the price at fifteen cents. The line is shorter. Every kid who wants a pencil gets one, and a few are left over. The class learns that a price is a kind of message. It tells buyers and sellers what to do next.
story.think: Was raising the price fair? What else could the class have done so that every kid got a pencil?

lessons.title: Producers and Consumers
lessons.mainIdea: Producers make goods or do services, and consumers buy and use them; most people are both.
reading: Think about a loaf of bread. A farmer grew the wheat. A mill ground it into flour. A baker mixed the dough and baked it. A truck driver carried it to the store. Each of those people is a *producer*. A producer is anyone who makes something or does work that others want.

Now think about who eats the bread. You do. The person who buys a loaf and uses it is a *consumer*. A consumer is someone who buys or uses goods and services. When you buy a pencil at the school store, you are a consumer. When your family buys gas for the car, they are consumers too.

Here is the surprising part. Almost everyone is both. The baker is a producer at work. On the way home, she buys shoes, so she is a consumer. Devon is a producer when he runs the store table. He is a consumer when he buys a pencil from it. Producers and consumers need each other.

words.d: a person or business that makes goods or does services that others want
a person who buys or uses goods and services

look.title: One Morning, Two Jobs
look.text: Mr. Kim fixes bikes in a shop on Western Avenue. At seven in the morning he buys coffee and a bagel. At eight he opens his shop and fixes a flat tire for a customer. At noon he buys lunch from the taco truck. At three he sells a used bike to a teenager.
look.prompt: List each moment when Mr. Kim is a producer and each moment when he is a consumer.

check.q: Which person is acting as a producer?
choices: A baker making bread to sell
check.why: A producer makes goods or does work that others want. The baker is making bread to sell.

check.q: When Devon buys a pencil at the store, what is he?
check.why: A consumer buys or uses goods and services. Buying a pencil makes Devon a consumer.

check.q: Why does the lesson say most people are both producers and consumers?
choices: Because only bakers can buy bread
Because people work and also buy things
check.why: People produce at their jobs and consume when they buy food, shoes and other things.

lessons.title: Goods and Services
lessons.mainIdea: Goods are things you can hold; services are work someone does for you.
reading: Walk through a shopping street. In one window there are shoes, bread and toys. Those are *goods*. A good is a thing you can touch and take home. A pencil is a good. So is a bike, an apple or a video game disc. Producers make goods in factories, on farms and in kitchens.

Next door is a barber shop. The barber does not sell you a thing to carry away. He cuts your hair. That is a *service*. A service is work that one person does for another. A doctor's visit, a bus ride, a haircut and a dog-walk are all services. Teachers, nurses and mail carriers all sell services.

Sometimes a business sells both. A pizza shop sells a pizza, which is a good. If the shop delivers it to your door, that delivery is a service. In Chicago, a huge share of jobs are in services, like health care, offices, restaurants and trucking. Fewer people make goods than in the past.

words.d: a thing that can be made, bought and touched, like a pencil or a bike
work that a person does for someone else, like a haircut or a bus ride

look.title: A Saturday List
look.text: On Saturday, Rosa's family bought a bag of apples, paid the dentist for a check-up, bought a new soccer ball, paid a plumber to fix a leaking sink and took the CTA bus downtown.
look.prompt: Sort each thing the family paid for into goods or services. Which list is longer?

check.q: Which of these is a service?
check.why: A service is work done for someone else. A haircut is work the barber does for you.

check.q: What is a good?
choices: A thing you can touch and take home
check.why: A good is a thing that can be made and touched, like an apple or a bike.

check.q: A pizza shop delivers a pizza to your house. What has it sold you?
check.why: The pizza is a good. The delivery is a service. The shop sold both.

lessons.title: Scarcity and the Choice You Give Up
lessons.mainIdea: Nothing is unlimited, so every choice means giving up the next best thing, called the opportunity cost.
reading: Maya has two dollars. She wants a notebook that costs two dollars and a pack of stickers that costs two dollars. She cannot buy both. This problem has a name: *scarcity*. Scarcity means there is not enough of something to do everything people want. Money is scarce. So is time, land and water.

Because of scarcity, every choice has a cost that is not printed on a tag. If Maya buys the notebook, she gives up the stickers. The stickers are her *opportunity cost*. The opportunity cost of a choice is the next best thing you did not pick. It is what you gave up.

Families, businesses and cities face this too. A city has a fixed budget. If it spends money on a new pool, it may not fix a street that year. The street is the opportunity cost of the pool. Good choosers name the opportunity cost out loud before they decide. That way they know what they are trading.

words.d: not having enough of something to do everything people want
the next best thing you give up when you make a choice

look.title: One Free Hour
look.text: Jalen has one free hour after dinner. He could practice piano, play basketball at the park, or finish a puzzle with his little sister. He picks basketball. The hour is gone.
look.prompt: What was the opportunity cost of Jalen's choice? Why can it only be one thing, not two?

check.q: What does scarcity mean?
choices: Not enough of something for all that people want
check.why: Scarcity means there is not enough of something, like money or time, to do everything people want.

check.q: Maya buys the notebook instead of the stickers. What is her opportunity cost?
check.why: The opportunity cost is the next best thing given up. Maya gave up the stickers.

check.q: A city spends its money on a pool and cannot fix a street. What is the street?
choices: The opportunity cost of the pool
check.why: The street repair is what the city gave up to build the pool. That is its opportunity cost.

lessons.title: Demand at the School Store
lessons.mainIdea: Demand is how much people want to buy at a price; when the price drops, more people buy.
reading: On the Friday of the big test, everyone wanted pencils. That wanting, joined with the money to pay, is called *demand*. Demand is how much of something people will buy at a certain price. On a normal Friday, demand for pencils is low. On test day, it shoots up.

Price changes demand too. At ten cents, kids bought three pencils each. At twenty-five cents, most would buy one. When the price goes down, people buy more. When the price goes up, people buy less. That pattern is so steady that economists call it a law.

Demand can also change for reasons that have nothing to do with price. A test makes demand rise. A snow day makes it fall to zero. If a famous singer holds a pencil in a video, demand might jump. A *market* is any place where buyers and sellers meet, and the school store is a tiny one.

words.d: how much of something people want and are able to buy at a price
any place where buyers and sellers come together to trade

look.title: Lemonade in Two Weathers
look.text: Two kids run a lemonade stand at fifty cents a cup. On a cool, cloudy day they sell six cups. On a hot day the next week, at the same price, they sell thirty cups. Then they raise the price to a dollar on another hot day and sell fifteen.
look.prompt: What changed demand between the first two days? What changed it on the third day?

check.q: What is demand?
choices: How much people will buy at a price
How many items a store has
The cost of making a good
check.why: Demand is how much of a good people want and can buy at a certain price.

check.q: If the price of a pencil goes up, what usually happens to the number sold?
check.why: When price rises, people buy less. That is the pattern the lesson calls a law.

check.q: Why did demand for pencils rise on test day?
choices: More kids wanted pencils that day
check.why: A test made more kids want pencils. Demand rose for a reason other than price.

lessons.title: Supply and Running Out
lessons.mainIdea: Supply is how much sellers offer; when supply is low and demand is high, the price tends to rise.
reading: The class had two hundred pencils. That number is the *supply*. Supply is how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a price. Sellers like higher prices. If pencils sold for a dollar, the class would order more boxes. If they sold for a penny, the class might not bother.

Now put supply and demand together. On test day, demand was high and supply was small. That is when a store runs out. The line got long. Some kids left empty-handed. A *shortage* is when buyers want more than sellers have at that price.

A higher price fixes a shortage in two ways. It makes some buyers take fewer. It makes sellers bring more. When the class raised the price to fifteen cents and ordered four hundred pencils, supply went up and demand went down. They met in the middle. That is what markets do every day, all over the world.

words.d: how much of something sellers are ready to sell at a price
when buyers want more of something than sellers have at that price

look.title: The Snow Shovel Problem
look.text: A hardware store in Rockford has twenty snow shovels. A storm drops a foot of snow overnight. By noon, two hundred people have come in asking for shovels. The owner has to decide what to do with the twenty on the shelf.
look.prompt: What is happening to demand and supply? What could the owner do, and who would be helped or hurt?

check.q: What is supply?
choices: How much sellers are ready to sell at a price
check.why: Supply is the amount sellers are willing to offer at a certain price.

check.q: What is a shortage?
choices: Too many pencils on the shelf
A day when the store is closed
A price that is too high
Buyers want more than sellers have at that price
check.why: A shortage happens when demand is greater than supply at the current price.

check.q: How does a higher price help end a shortage?
choices: Buyers take fewer and sellers bring more
check.why: A higher price makes some buyers take less and gives sellers a reason to supply more.

lessons.title: What a Price Tells You
lessons.mainIdea: A price is a signal that tells buyers how to spend and sellers what to make.
reading: A *price* is the amount of money you trade for a good or service. But a price is also a message. When strawberries cost six dollars a box in January, the price says they are hard to get right now. In June, when Illinois farms are picking, the price drops to two dollars. The price says: plenty here, buy now.

Sellers read prices too. When pencils sold out fast at ten cents, the price was telling the class it was set too low. When the price of corn is high, farmers plant more corn. When it falls, some switch to soybeans. No one has to order them. The price does the talking.

Prices are not perfect. A price does not say whether something is good for you. It does not say whether a family can afford it. That is why people also use rules, taxes and help for people in need. But as a quick way to move goods to the people who want them most, a price is a powerful tool.

words.d: the amount of money traded for a good or service
a message that tells people what is happening and what to do

look.title: Why the Baker Bakes
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776
look.prompt: Benevolence means kindness. Smith says the baker bakes for his own reasons, not just to be nice. How does that still end up feeding you?

check.q: In June, Illinois strawberries cost less than in January. What is the price telling you?
choices: There are plenty of strawberries right now
check.why: A low price signals that a good is plentiful. In June, local farms are picking.

check.q: When corn prices are high, what do farmers tend to do?
check.why: A high price tells sellers to make more. Farmers plant more corn when it pays well.

check.q: What is one thing a price does NOT tell you?
choices: That a good is scarce right now
Whether a family can afford it
check.why: A price is a signal about how scarce a good is, but it says nothing about who can afford it.

lessons.title: Earn, Save, Spend, Give
lessons.mainIdea: Money you earn can be spent, saved for later or given away, and a budget helps you plan all three.
reading: Amara walks her neighbor's dog every afternoon. Each week she gets ten dollars. That is *earning*. People earn money by producing something, from a dog-walk to a day at a factory. Some people earn a wage by the hour. Some earn a salary by the year. Some own a business and keep what is left after costs.

Amara has a plan for her ten dollars. Four go in a jar for a bike she wants by summer. That is *saving*, keeping money now to use later. Five she spends on snacks and a book. One she puts in a can at her mosque for families who need food. That is giving. Many families give to a church, a temple or a food pantry.

Her plan is a *budget*. A budget is a written plan for money coming in and going out. It is simple math, but it changes lives. If Amara skipped the plan, she might spend all ten and never get the bike. Writing down the plan makes the opportunity cost of every snack easy to see.

words.d: to get money in return for work you do
to keep money now so you can use it later
a written plan for the money you will earn, spend, save and give

look.title: Amara's Weekly Plan
look.prompt: If the bike costs one hundred dollars, about how many weeks will Amara need? What could she change to get there sooner?

check.q: What is saving?
choices: Keeping money now to use later
check.why: Saving means holding on to money now so you can use it for something later.

check.q: Which of these is earning?
choices: Putting four dollars in a jar
Getting ten dollars for walking a dog
Dropping a dollar in a donation can
check.why: Earning is getting money in return for work. Amara works by walking the dog.

check.q: Why does a budget help Amara?
choices: It makes money grow by itself
It shows her plan so she reaches her goal
check.why: A budget is a plan. It makes the cost of each choice clear so she can reach the bike.

lessons.title: What a Bank Does
lessons.mainIdea: A bank keeps money safe, pays savers interest and lends money to people who need it now.
reading: A jar under the bed is a risky place for one hundred dollars. It can be lost, stolen or spent on a whim. So people take money to a *bank*. A bank is a business that keeps money safe. When you put money in, the bank writes down what it owes you. That is your account. You can take it out when you need it.

The bank does not leave your money in a pile. It lends most of it to other people. A family borrows to buy a house. A baker borrows to buy a bigger oven. They pay the money back over time, plus extra. That extra is *interest*. Interest is the price of using someone else's money.

The bank shares some of that interest with you for letting it use your savings. So a savings account grows a little every year. In the United States, a government program insures bank accounts up to a set amount. If a bank fails, savers still get their money. That rule came after many banks closed in the 1930s.

words.d: a business that keeps money safe, pays interest to savers and lends money
the extra money paid for using someone else's money

look.title: The Bakery Oven
look.text: Ms. Lopez owns a small bakery in Aurora. Her one oven is too small for all her orders. A new oven costs eight thousand dollars. She has two thousand saved. A bank offers to lend her the rest if she pays it back over three years with interest.
look.prompt: What does Ms. Lopez gain by borrowing? What does she risk? Where does the bank get the money to lend her?

check.q: Where does a bank get most of the money it lends?
check.why: A bank lends out money that savers have put in their accounts.

check.q: What is interest?
choices: Extra money paid for using someone else's money
check.why: Interest is the price of borrowing. Borrowers pay it, and savers earn some of it.

check.q: Why does a savings account grow a little each year?
choices: The bank pays interest on your savings
The bank adds coins for fun
Money always grows in a jar
check.why: The bank shares some interest with savers for letting it use their money.

lessons.title: Taxes and Public Goods
lessons.mainIdea: Taxes are money people pay to the government so it can provide public goods that everyone shares.
reading: Who paid for the street outside your school? Who pays the firefighters? No single family could buy a fire truck. So people pool their money through *taxes*. A tax is money that people and businesses must pay to a government. In Illinois, the state adds a sales tax to most things you buy. Workers pay a tax on what they earn. Homeowners pay a tax on their houses.

That money buys *public goods*. A public good is something everyone can use and no one can be kept from using, like a road, a park, a streetlight or clean air. A store cannot sell a streetlight one glow at a time. So governments provide it and taxes pay for it. Public schools, libraries and fire protection are paid the same way.

People argue about taxes all the time. Some say taxes are too high and take money families could use. Others say they are too low to fix roads and pay teachers. Both sides are talking about opportunity cost. Every tax dollar spent on one thing is not spent on another, and every dollar not collected is a public good not built.

words.d: money that people and businesses must pay to a government
something everyone can use and share, like a road or a park, that taxes pay for

look.title: The Power to Tax
look.text: The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States.
look.cite: United States Constitution, Article I, Section 8, 1787
look.prompt: What two reasons does the Constitution give for collecting taxes? Name one public good that fits each reason.

check.q: What is a tax?
choices: Money people must pay to a government
check.why: A tax is money that people and businesses are required to pay to a government.

check.q: Which of these is a public good?
check.why: A streetlight can be used by everyone and no one can be kept from using it.

check.q: Why do governments, not stores, provide streetlights?
choices: You cannot sell a streetlight's glow to one buyer
check.why: A public good cannot be sold one piece at a time, so taxes pay for it and everyone shares.

lessons.title: Corn Here, Oranges There
lessons.mainIdea: Specialization means doing what you do best, and regions specialize because of their land and climate.
reading: Drive across central Illinois in August and you see corn for miles. Fly to Florida and you see orange groves. Why not the other way around? Illinois has deep, dark soil and warm, rainy summers. Corn loves that. Florida is warm all winter. Orange trees die in a hard freeze, so they need a place that stays warm.

This is *specialization*. To specialize is to focus on the thing you can do best. Illinois specializes in corn and soybeans. Florida specializes in oranges. Idaho grows potatoes. Wisconsin makes cheese. Each place makes more by doing what its land and weather favor, instead of trying to grow a little of everything.

People specialize too. In Room 210, Maya is best with money and Devon is best with counting. So Maya keeps the box and Devon keeps the stock. A dentist does not bake her own bread. She fixes teeth all day and buys bread with what she earns. Specializing lets each person get very good at one thing.

words.d: focusing on making the thing you can do best
the usual weather of a place over many years

look.title: Average January Temperature
look.cite: National Weather Service climate normals, rounded
look.prompt: Orange trees die when it stays below freezing (32 degrees) for long. Use the numbers to explain why Florida, not Illinois, grows oranges.

check.q: Why does Illinois grow so much corn?
choices: It has deep soil and rainy summers
check.why: Corn grows well in the deep soil and warm, rainy summers of Illinois.

check.q: What is specialization?
choices: Focusing on what you do best
check.why: To specialize is to focus on the thing a person or place can do best.

check.q: Why do orange trees not grow well in Illinois?
choices: There is too much rain in summer
check.why: Orange trees die in a hard freeze. Illinois winters are far below freezing.

lessons.title: Why Trade Makes Both Sides Better
lessons.mainIdea: When people and places specialize and then trade, each ends up with more than it could make alone.
reading: Specialization only works if you can *trade*. To trade is to give something you have for something you want. Illinois sends corn and soybeans down the Mississippi River and across the world. Trucks and trains bring back oranges, cars, phones and shoes. Without trade, Illinois families would have no oranges at all.

Trade works because both sides win. Think of lunch. Sam has two bags of grapes and no crackers. Leo has two packs of crackers and no grapes. Each trades one for one. Now each has grapes and crackers. Nobody lost. The same thing happens when a country trades wheat for coffee.

Trade also has costs, and people argue about them. When a factory moves to another country, workers here can lose jobs. Goods get cheaper for consumers, but some producers are hurt. Both sides of that argument use real evidence. Knowing that trade makes the whole pie bigger does not tell you who gets each slice.

words.d: giving something you have in exchange for something you want
a good sent out of a place to be sold somewhere else

look.title: Two Farms, One Fence
look.text: Farm A can grow one thousand bushels of corn or two hundred bushels of apples in a year. Farm B, on a hilly slope, can grow two hundred bushels of corn or one thousand bushels of apples. Each farm wants both corn and apples.
look.prompt: What should each farm grow? What should they do next? Would they have more or less if each tried to grow both?

check.q: What is trade?
choices: Giving something you have for something you want
check.why: Trade is exchanging something you have for something you want.

check.q: Sam trades grapes for Leo's crackers. Who is better off?
check.why: Each gave up something they had extra of and got something they wanted. Both gained.

check.q: What is one real cost of trade the lesson mentions?
choices: Some workers here can lose jobs
check.why: When production moves elsewhere, some local workers lose jobs even though consumers pay less.

lessons.title: Starting Something New
lessons.mainIdea: An entrepreneur takes a risk to start a business that solves a problem people will pay for.
reading: In the early 1900s, a young man named Richard Sears sold watches by mail from a small railroad station. Later, with a partner, he built a company in Chicago. It mailed a thick catalog to farm families. They could order a stove, a dress or even a whole house kit. Sears saw a problem. Farm families lived far from stores. He found a way to solve it.

Sears was an *entrepreneur*. An entrepreneur is a person who starts a business, taking the *risk* that it might fail. Risk means the chance of losing something. Entrepreneurs put in their own money, time and sleep. Many businesses do fail. The ones that succeed create jobs and new goods and services.

You do not need to be famous to be one. The kids with the lemonade stand are entrepreneurs. So is the teenager who fixes phones after school. An entrepreneur looks for a need that is not being met, thinks of a way to meet it and tries. Room 210's store began that way, with one question: what do kids keep running out of?

words.d: a person who starts a business and takes the risk that it might fail
the chance of losing something, like money or time

look.title: The Problem on Your Block
look.text: On Tasha's block, older neighbors cannot carry heavy grocery bags up their stairs. Tasha and two friends have a wagon and free time on Saturdays. They think they could charge two dollars per trip. But they will need a sign, and they might spend a Saturday waiting with no customers.
look.prompt: What need did Tasha spot? What is her risk? What would you tell her to find out before she starts?

check.q: What is an entrepreneur?
choices: A person who only buys goods
A person who starts a business and takes a risk
check.why: An entrepreneur starts a business, knowing it might fail.

check.q: What problem did Richard Sears solve?
choices: Farm families lived far from stores
check.why: Sears mailed a catalog so farm families far from stores could order what they needed.

check.q: What does risk mean in this lesson?
check.why: Risk is the chance that you lose money, time or effort if the business fails.

review.q: A farmer grows wheat and a mill grinds it into flour. Both are what?
review.why: Producers make goods or do work that others want. Both the farmer and the mill are producers.

review.q: Which of these is a good, not a service?
review.why: A good is a thing you can touch and take home. A bike is a good.

review.q: Why can't Maya buy both the notebook and the stickers?
review.why: Scarcity means she does not have enough money for everything she wants.

review.q: On test day the school store ran out of pencils. What was happening?
review.why: A shortage is when buyers want more than sellers have at that price.

review.q: The price of strawberries falls in June. What does the price signal?
review.why: A low price signals that a good is easy to get right now.

review.q: Money paid for using someone else's money is called what?
review.why: Interest is the price of borrowing. Banks pay it to savers and charge it to borrowers.

review.q: Which is the best example of a public good paid for by taxes?
review.why: A park can be used by everyone and is paid for by taxes, so it is a public good.

review.q: Why do Illinois and Florida grow different crops?
choices: Their land and climate favor different crops
The government tells them what to grow
review.why: Places specialize in what their soil and climate favor: corn in Illinois, oranges in Florida.

chapters.title: Regions of the United States
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the land, water and weather of a place shape how people there live and work?

story.title: A Truck Full of Corn
story.kicker: One load of Illinois corn rolls from a farm field to a river, then a thousand miles to the sea.
paragraphs: It is a cold morning in October near Peoria, Illinois. A combine has been chewing through cornfields for a week. Now a red truck sits under the combine's spout. Yellow kernels pour in like a waterfall. The farmer, Ms. Duffy, checks the load. About nine hundred bushels. She climbs into the cab and pulls out onto the county road.

Twenty minutes later she reaches the grain elevator on the Illinois River. A worker weighs the truck. Then the corn rushes down into a huge concrete tower. Ms. Duffy is paid by the bushel. Her corn joins the corn of hundreds of other farms. None of it will stay in Illinois. Most of it is headed for other countries.

At the river, a long metal barge waits. A single barge carries as much corn as about sixty trucks. Fifteen barges are tied together and pushed by one towboat. The tow moves slowly down the Illinois River. It joins the Mississippi River above St. Louis. Then it turns south.

The river grows wider. The tow passes Memphis, Tennessee. The air gets warmer and heavy with moisture. Ten days after leaving Illinois, the tow reaches the busy docks near New Orleans, Louisiana. Giant machines lift the corn into an ocean ship. That ship may sail to Mexico, to Japan or to Egypt.

Back in Peoria, Ms. Duffy is already planning next year. She reads the price of corn on her phone. She checks the weather. She looks at a map of the river. Her farm is in the middle of the country, far from any ocean. But because of the rivers, her corn can reach the whole world.
story.think: Why does corn from the middle of the country travel by river instead of by truck the whole way? What would change if the river were not there?

lessons.title: Lines Around the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: Latitude lines measure how far north or south a place is, and longitude lines measure east or west.
reading: Imagine the Earth as a ball with a net drawn on it. Some lines run side to side. Those are lines of *latitude*. The middle line is the equator. It is zero degrees. Lines north of it are labeled north, up to ninety degrees at the North Pole. Chicago sits at about forty-two degrees north.

Other lines run up and down from pole to pole. Those are lines of *longitude*. The zero line, called the prime meridian, passes through Greenwich, England. Lines are counted east or west from there. Chicago is about eighty-eight degrees west. So Chicago's address on the Earth is forty-two north, eighty-eight west.

Latitude also hints at weather. Places near the equator are usually hot. Places far north or south are cold. Miami, Florida, is at about twenty-six degrees north. Chicago is much farther north, so Chicago has snowy winters and Miami almost never sees snow. Sailors, pilots and phone maps all use these two numbers to find any spot on Earth.

words.d: lines that run side to side and measure how far north or south a place is from the equator
lines that run from pole to pole and measure how far east or west a place is
the line of zero latitude that circles the middle of the Earth

look.title: How Far North?
look.prompt: Which city on the list is closest to the equator? Which two Illinois cities are near each other? What would you guess about their winters?

check.q: Which lines measure how far north or south a place is?
check.why: Latitude lines run side to side and count degrees north or south of the equator.

check.q: What is the equator?
choices: The line at ninety degrees north
The zero line of latitude around the middle of Earth
check.why: The equator is zero degrees latitude and circles the middle of the Earth.

check.q: Chicago is at forty-two north and Miami at twenty-six north. What does that tell you?
choices: Miami is farther from the equator
Chicago is farther north and colder
check.why: A higher north latitude means farther from the equator and usually colder winters.

lessons.title: How Big Is It Really?
lessons.mainIdea: Map scale tells you how much real distance one inch on the map stands for.
reading: A map of Illinois fits on one page. The real Illinois is almost four hundred miles from top to bottom. How can that work? Every map is shrunk by the same amount. The *scale* tells you how much. A scale might say one inch equals fifty miles. Then a two-inch gap on the map means one hundred real miles.

Most maps show scale as a small bar with numbers, like a tiny ruler. To use it, measure the distance between two towns on the map with a strip of paper. Then hold the strip against the scale bar and read the miles. On a road map, that tells you how long a drive will be.

Scale changes with the map. A map of your school might use one inch for twenty feet. A map of the whole country might use one inch for two hundred miles. On that big map, Chicago is just a dot. On a city map, Chicago fills the whole page and you can see every street. Big area, small scale. Small area, big detail.

words.d: the part of a map that tells how much real distance one inch on the map stands for
how far it is from one place to another

look.title: Two Inches to Springfield
look.text: On a map of Illinois, the scale bar says one inch equals one hundred miles. Chicago and Springfield are about two inches apart on the map. Chicago and Cairo, at the far southern tip, are about three and a half inches apart.
look.prompt: About how many real miles is Springfield from Chicago? About how far is Cairo? Which drive would take longer?

check.q: A map scale says one inch equals fifty miles. Two towns are three inches apart. How far apart are they?
check.why: Three inches times fifty miles per inch equals one hundred fifty miles.

check.q: What does a map's scale tell you?
choices: How the map is shrunk from real size
check.why: Scale tells how much real distance each inch on the map stands for.

check.q: Which map would show every street in Chicago?
choices: A map of the whole United States
A map of the city alone
check.why: A map of a small area can show more detail. A city map shows streets; a country map shows a dot.

lessons.title: Physical Maps and Political Maps
lessons.mainIdea: A physical map shows land and water; a political map shows borders, states and cities that people made.
reading: Open two maps of the United States side by side. On the first, you see brown mountains, green lowlands and blue rivers. There are no state lines. This is a *physical map*. It shows things nature made: mountains, plains, deserts, lakes, rivers and coasts. The Rocky Mountains show up as a long brown ridge down the west.

On the second map, the land is divided into fifty colored shapes with names. Dots mark cities. Stars mark capitals. This is a *political map*. It shows things people decided: state borders, country borders, cities and capitals. A state line is invisible on the ground. You only see it on a political map.

Some borders follow nature and some do not. The Mississippi River is the western edge of Illinois, so that border wiggles like the river. The northern edge of Illinois is a straight line drawn by lawmakers in 1818. Reading both kinds of maps together tells you the most. You can see why Chicago sits where Lake Michigan meets the prairie.

words.d: a map that shows land and water features made by nature
a map that shows borders, states, countries and cities that people made
the line where one state or country ends and another begins

look.title: The Shape of Illinois
look.text: Look at the outline of Illinois. The west side is wavy from top to bottom. The south comes to a point. The east side is straight at the top and wavy at the bottom. The north is one straight line.
look.prompt: Which sides of Illinois probably follow rivers? Which sides did people draw with a ruler? How could a physical map help you check?

check.q: Which map would show the Rocky Mountains but no state lines?
check.why: A physical map shows land and water made by nature, not borders made by people.

check.q: What does a political map show?
check.why: A political map shows things people decided, like state borders and capitals.

check.q: Why does the western border of Illinois wiggle?
choices: Lawmakers drew it that way for fun
check.why: The western edge of Illinois is the Mississippi River, so the border bends with the river.

lessons.title: The Northeast
lessons.mainIdea: The Northeast is a small, crowded region of old cities, rocky coasts and the Appalachian Mountains.
reading: The United States is huge, so people sort it into five *regions*. A region is an area where places share things, like landforms, weather or history. The Northeast is the smallest region by land. It runs from Maine down to Pennsylvania. It touches the Atlantic Ocean, and its coast is rocky in the north and sandy in the south.

The Appalachian Mountains run through the Northeast. They are old, rounded mountains covered in forest. Winters are cold and snowy. Fall turns the hills red and gold. Rivers cut through the mountains to the sea. Early towns grew where rivers could turn mill wheels.

The Northeast has the biggest city in the country. New York City has about eight million people. Boston and Philadelphia are old port cities from before the American Revolution. Today many people there work in offices, banks, hospitals and universities. Fishing boats still leave from Maine and Massachusetts harbors. They have done so for four hundred years.

words.d: an area where the places share features like land, weather or history
the land along the edge of an ocean or sea

look.title: Biggest Cities by Region
look.prompt: About how many times bigger is New York City than Chicago? Which region's largest city is the smallest on this list?

check.q: What is a region?
choices: An area where places share features
check.why: A region is an area where the places share landforms, weather or history.

check.q: Which mountains run through the Northeast?
check.why: The old, forested Appalachian Mountains run through the Northeast.

check.q: Which is the largest city in the United States?
check.why: New York City in the Northeast has about eight million people, the most of any U.S. city.

lessons.title: The Southeast
lessons.mainIdea: The Southeast is warm and wet, with long coasts, wide rivers and farms that grow crops the North cannot.
reading: Step off a plane in Atlanta, Georgia, in July. The air feels like a warm, wet towel. The Southeast has hot, *humid* summers and mild winters. Humid means the air holds a lot of water. Rain is heavy. That is why the region is so green, with pine forests, swamps and the wide grassy wetland in Florida called the Everglades.

Two coasts wrap the Southeast. The Atlantic is on the east. The Gulf of Mexico is on the south. The Mississippi River ends here, spreading into a delta near New Orleans. The northern part has the southern end of the Appalachian Mountains. The Smoky Mountains in Tennessee and North Carolina are the tallest in the east.

The warm weather lets farmers grow oranges, peanuts, cotton and rice. Ports like New Orleans and Savannah ship goods around the world. Millions of visitors come for beaches and theme parks. But the warm ocean that draws tourists also feeds hurricanes. These huge storms hit the coast most years between June and November.

words.d: air that holds a lot of water, making it feel wet and heavy
land built up from mud where a river spreads out and enters the sea

look.title: A Field in Two Places
look.text: A farmer in southern Georgia plants peanuts in April and picks them in September. The ground never freezes hard in winter. A farmer near Rockford, Illinois, cannot plant anything until the frost ends in May, and the ground freezes solid in January.
look.prompt: How does the Southeast's climate change what a farmer can grow and when? What crops could the Illinois farmer grow that the Georgia farmer might not?

check.q: What does humid mean?
choices: Air that holds a lot of water
check.why: Humid air holds lots of water, which makes Southeast summers feel wet and heavy.

check.q: Which two bodies of water border the Southeast?
choices: The Pacific Ocean and Lake Michigan
The Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico
The Great Lakes and Hudson Bay
The Arctic Ocean and the Gulf
check.why: The Atlantic is on the east side of the Southeast and the Gulf of Mexico is on the south.

check.q: What danger comes with the warm ocean water of the Southeast?
check.why: Warm ocean water feeds hurricanes, which hit the Southeast coast most years.

lessons.title: The Southwest and the West
lessons.mainIdea: The Southwest is mostly hot and dry; the West has the tallest mountains, the Pacific coast and the most varied land.
reading: The Southwest is Texas, Oklahoma, New Mexico and Arizona. Much of it is *desert*, land that gets very little rain. Cactus grows where corn cannot. The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon in Arizona, a gorge about a mile deep. The Rio Grande forms the border with Mexico. Cities like Phoenix and Houston have grown fast, and water is the region's biggest worry.

The West is the biggest region. It reaches from the Rocky Mountains to the Pacific Ocean, and also includes Alaska and Hawaii. The Rockies are tall and jagged. Farther west, the Sierra Nevada and the Cascade Range rise near the coast. Between them lie dry basins and Death Valley, the lowest and hottest spot in the country.

Because the land is so varied, so is the work. California's Central Valley grows a huge share of the nation's fruit, nuts and vegetables. Washington and Oregon cut lumber and grow apples. Alaska catches fish and pumps oil. Los Angeles makes movies and Seattle makes software. The West also has earthquakes, wildfires and even volcanoes, like Mount St. Helens.

words.d: land that gets very little rain, so few plants can grow
a deep, narrow valley with steep sides cut by a river

look.title: Highest Point in Each Region
look.prompt: Which region has the tallest mountain? About how many times taller is Mount Whitney than the highest point in Illinois?

check.q: What is a desert?
choices: Land that gets very little rain
check.why: A desert gets very little rain, so only tough plants like cactus can grow there.

check.q: Which river carved the Grand Canyon?
check.why: The Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon in Arizona over millions of years.

check.q: Which region includes Alaska and Hawaii?
check.why: The West is the largest region and includes Alaska and Hawaii along with the Pacific states.

lessons.title: The Heart of the Country
lessons.mainIdea: The Midwest is flat, fertile land between the Great Lakes and the Great Plains, crossed by big rivers.
reading: Stand in a field in central Iowa and turn all the way around. The land is nearly flat to every horizon. This is the Midwest. It stretches from Ohio to the Dakotas. Long ago, sheets of ice called glaciers pushed across this land and ground it flat. When they melted, they left rich, dark soil. That soil is the region's treasure.

The Midwest has some of the biggest fresh water on Earth. The five Great Lakes sit along its northern edge. Lake Michigan is the only one entirely inside the United States. Three great rivers cross the region: the Mississippi, the Missouri and the Ohio. To the west, the land rises slowly into the dry grassland of the Great Plains.

Winters are cold and summers are hot. Farmers grow corn and soybeans and raise hogs and cattle. Wisconsin makes cheese. Cities like Chicago, Detroit and Minneapolis grew up around factories, railroads and lake ports. People in Illinois say they live in the *heartland*, a word for the middle of a country where much of its food is grown.

words.d: a huge, slow-moving sheet of ice
the central part of a country, often where much of its food is grown
wide, flat land with few trees

look.title: Amber Waves of Grain
look.text: O beautiful for spacious skies, For amber waves of grain, For purple mountain majesties Above the fruited plain!
look.cite: Katharine Lee Bates, the poem America the Beautiful, published 1895
look.prompt: Bates wrote this after a train trip across the country. Which region do amber waves of grain describe? Which region has purple mountains?

check.q: What left the Midwest flat with rich soil?
choices: Glaciers that pushed across it and melted
check.why: Sheets of ice ground the land flat and left dark, fertile soil when they melted.

check.q: Which Great Lake lies entirely inside the United States?
check.why: Lake Michigan is the only Great Lake that does not touch Canada.

check.q: What does heartland mean?
choices: The central part of a country where much food is grown
check.why: Heartland means the middle of a country, and the Midwest grows much of the nation's food.

lessons.title: Illinois Up Close
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois is a long, mostly flat state framed by rivers and a Great Lake, with a giant city in one corner.
reading: Illinois is shaped like a long arrowhead pointing south. Water frames almost every side. Lake Michigan touches the northeast corner. The Mississippi River runs down the whole west side. The Ohio River is the southern tip. The Wabash River makes much of the eastern edge. The Illinois River cuts through the middle from northeast to southwest.

Most of the state was once *prairie*, a sea of tall grass with almost no trees. Farmers plowed it into cornfields. The highest point, Charles Mound in the northwest corner, is only about 1,235 feet high. The southern tip has low, wooded hills called the Shawnee Hills. It is warmer down there, closer to Kentucky than to Chicago.

Two cities matter most. Springfield, in the middle, is the *capital*, where the state's laws are made. Chicago, in the corner, is home to about 2.7 million people and is the biggest city between the coasts. The state has about 12.8 million people, and most live in the Chicago area. That is why Illinois is both a farm state and a big-city state.

words.d: wide, flat land covered in tall grass with few trees
the city where a state's or country's government meets

look.title: Rivers That Touch Illinois
look.prompt: Which of these rivers lies entirely inside Illinois? Why do you think early towns like Peoria and Cairo grew on rivers?

check.q: Which river runs down the whole west side of Illinois?
check.why: The Mississippi River forms the entire western border of Illinois.

check.q: What is a prairie?
choices: Flat land covered in tall grass
check.why: A prairie is wide, flat grassland with few trees. Most of Illinois was prairie.

check.q: Where are Illinois laws made?
check.why: Springfield is the capital, where the state government meets.

lessons.title: Jobs and Food From the Land
lessons.mainIdea: The natural resources of a region decide much of what people there grow, make and do for work.
reading: Why does Maine have lobster boats and Kansas have wheat combines? The answer is *natural resources*. A natural resource is something useful found in nature, like soil, water, trees, fish, oil or minerals. Each region has a different mix. People build jobs around the resources close at hand.

The Midwest's resource is soil, so it grows grain and feeds animals. The Southeast has warmth and rain, so it grows oranges and peanuts. The Southwest has oil under Texas and Oklahoma, so many people there drill and refine it. The West has forests, fish and long growing seasons in California. The Northeast has deep harbors, so it became a center of shipping and trade.

Resources shape food too. A Chicago hot dog, a Texas barbecue, a Louisiana gumbo full of shrimp and a Maine lobster roll each come from what was nearby. But resources are not the whole story. Chicago has no oil and no ocean. It became a giant city because railroads and Lake Michigan met there, and people brought the resources to it.

words.d: something useful found in nature, like soil, water, trees, fish or oil
a solid material dug from the earth, like iron, coal or salt

look.title: Match the Job to the Place
look.text: Here are five jobs: an orange picker, a lobster fisher, a corn farmer, an oil rig worker and a lumberjack. Here are five places: the Maine coast, a Texas oil field, a Florida grove, a Washington forest and a central Illinois farm.
look.prompt: Match each job to its place. What natural resource makes each job possible there and not somewhere else?

check.q: What is a natural resource?
check.why: Natural resources are useful things from nature, such as soil, water, trees, fish and oil.

check.q: Why is oil drilling a big job in the Southwest?
choices: Oil lies under Texas and Oklahoma
check.why: People build jobs around nearby resources, and oil is found under Texas and Oklahoma.

check.q: Chicago has no oil and no ocean. Why did it become a giant city?
choices: Railroads and Lake Michigan met there
check.why: Chicago grew where rail lines and the lake came together, so resources were brought to it.

lessons.title: Moving People and Goods
lessons.mainIdea: Rivers, rails, highways and airports connect the regions and make Illinois a crossroads of the country.
reading: Ms. Duffy's corn traveled by truck, then barge, then ocean ship. Each way of moving things is a kind of *transportation*. Barges are the cheapest way to move heavy loads like grain and coal. Trains are next. Trucks can go anywhere there is a road. Airplanes are the fastest and most expensive, so they carry people, mail and small valuable things.

Illinois sits where all of these meet. The Illinois Waterway links Lake Michigan to the Mississippi River, so a boat can go from Chicago to the Gulf of Mexico. More freight trains pass through Chicago than any other city in the country. Interstate highways cross the state in every direction. O'Hare Airport in Chicago is one of the busiest in the world.

This is not luck. In the 1800s, workers dug a canal from Chicago to the Illinois River. Then railroads chose Chicago as the place where eastern and western lines met. Being a *hub*, a center where routes come together, gave Chicago jobs in warehouses, rail yards and trucking that still exist today. Geography drew the map, and people built on it.

words.d: the ways people and goods are moved from place to place
a center where many routes come together
a waterway dug by people so boats can travel

look.title: A River Worth Knowing
look.text: Mark Twain opened his book about the Mississippi by saying the river was well worth reading about, because it was not an ordinary river but remarkable in every way. He went on to describe how much of the country's water it drains and how far it carries boats.
look.cite: Mark Twain, Life on the Mississippi, 1883 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Twain was a riverboat pilot before he was a writer. Why might a river have seemed like the most important road in the country in the 1800s?

check.q: Which way of moving heavy grain is cheapest?
check.why: Barges carry huge loads for the least cost, so they move most grain and coal.

check.q: What does the Illinois Waterway connect?
choices: Lake Michigan and the Mississippi River
The Rocky Mountains and the coast
check.why: The waterway links Lake Michigan to the Mississippi so boats can reach the Gulf of Mexico.

check.q: What is a hub?
choices: A center where many routes meet
check.why: A hub is a center where routes come together, like Chicago for railroads and highways.

lessons.title: When Nature Strikes
lessons.mainIdea: Each region faces its own natural hazards, and people prepare for the ones most likely where they live.
reading: A *natural hazard* is a danger that comes from nature. Every region has some, but not the same ones. The Southeast gets hurricanes from the warm ocean. The West gets earthquakes, where the ground shakes, and wildfires in dry summers. The Southwest faces long droughts, years with too little rain. The Northeast gets blizzards and ice storms.

The Midwest has *tornadoes*, spinning funnels of wind that drop from storm clouds. They form where warm, wet air from the Gulf meets cold, dry air from the north. Illinois gets dozens most years, mostly in spring. The Midwest also gets floods when the big rivers rise. In 1993 the Mississippi flooded for months and covered farms and towns along the Illinois shore.

Because the hazards differ, so do the plans. Florida homes have shutters for hurricanes. California buildings are built to bend in an earthquake. Illinois schools practice tornado drills, moving to inner hallways away from windows. Knowing your region's hazard is the first step in staying safe. The second step is a plan your family has talked through.

words.d: a danger that comes from nature, like a storm, flood or earthquake
a spinning funnel of wind that drops from a storm cloud
a long time with too little rain

look.title: Three Sirens
look.text: In Joliet, Illinois, a siren sounds on a warm April afternoon and the sky turns green. In Miami, the news warns of a storm coming in three days and people board up windows. In Los Angeles, dishes rattle for ten seconds with no warning at all.
look.prompt: Name the hazard in each place. Which one gives the most warning? Which gives the least? How does that change how people prepare?

check.q: Which hazard is most common in the Midwest?
check.why: Tornadoes form where warm Gulf air meets cold northern air over the Midwest.

check.q: What is a drought?
choices: A long time with too little rain
check.why: A drought is a long stretch with too little rain, a major hazard in the Southwest.

check.q: Why do Illinois schools practice tornado drills instead of hurricane drills?
choices: Tornadoes are the hazard most likely in Illinois
check.why: People prepare for the hazard most likely in their region. In Illinois that is tornadoes.

review.q: Which lines run side to side and measure north and south?
review.why: Latitude lines measure how far north or south a place is from the equator.

review.q: A map scale says one inch equals one hundred miles. Two cities are two inches apart. How far apart are they?
review.why: Two inches times one hundred miles per inch equals two hundred miles.

review.q: Which kind of map shows state borders and capitals?
review.why: A political map shows things people made, like borders, states and capitals.

review.q: Which region has hot, humid summers, two coasts and hurricanes?
review.why: The Southeast borders the Atlantic and the Gulf and gets hurricanes from warm ocean water.

review.q: Which region includes the Grand Canyon and much desert?
review.why: The Southwest is mostly dry, and the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

review.q: What is the capital of Illinois?
review.why: Springfield, in the middle of the state, is where Illinois laws are made.

review.q: Why did Chicago become a transportation hub?
choices: Railroads and Lake Michigan met there
review.why: Rail lines from east and west met at the lake, and a canal linked the lake to the rivers.

review.q: A region's natural resources mostly decide what?
choices: The jobs and food people there have
How many degrees of latitude it covers
review.why: People build jobs around nearby resources, and local food comes from what is close at hand.
